latin.369: §. III. Utriusque Consubstantiationis Historiam, per Compendiolum aliquod tradendum, tribus admodum momentis comprehendemus, quorum primum Consubstantiationis CONCEPTIONEM; Secundum, NATIVITATEM; Tertium, PERDURATIONEM enarrat.
latin.370: CONCEPTIONEM locandam arbitramur in triplici errore eorum, qui Consubstantiationem alterutram enixi tandèm sunt. Horum errorum PRIMUM absolvunt malè intellecta Patrum primorum Dicta, vel, ex duabus rebus, id est Substantiis, terrena, & cælesti, vel ex una tantum terrena substantia, at Accidente quodam Cælesti, sive Externæ Sanctitatis, sive Virtutis Divinæ Intrinsecæ, adaucta, Eucharistiam sacram constare innuentium.
latin.371: (1) Duas hîc Substantias memorat unus omnium instar Irenæus Anno Dni. 160: Panis, inquit, qui est à terra, percipiens invocationem Dei, jam non communis panis est, sed Eucharistia ex duabus rebus constans, terrena & cælesti, libro 4. contra hæres. cap. 34.; Sed libro 5. cap. 12. idem ferè repetens, adjicit tamen, se verba sua ad usum sacræ Eucharistiæ restricta velle, in quo fiat, ut quemadmodum animæ cælestes, cælesti substantia, ceu alimento sibi proprio, sic corpora terrestria substantia terrestri nutriantur & augescant: Eum, inquit, Calicem, qui est creatura, suum sanguinem, & eum panem, qui est creatura, suum corpus confirmavit: Quando ergo calix & panis percipiunt verbum Dei, fit Eucharistia sanguinis & corporis Christi ex quibus augetur & consistit Carnis nostræ substantia.
latin.372: (2) Substantiam terrenam sanctitate quadam affectam, Irenæo paulò vetustior Scriptor, S. Justinus Martyr, saltem implicitè inducit, quando Apol. secunda ad Anton. Imperat. prope finem, Christianorum sui temporis consuetudinem celebrandæ Cænæ hisce recenset: Postquam Præses gratias egit & acclamavit populus, illi, qui à nobis dicuntur Diaconi, seu Ministri, dant cuique præsentium quod sumant de pane & vino; & hoc alimentum à nobis vocatur Eucharistia; non enim ut vulgarem panem, neque ut vulgare poculum ea sumimus. Eundem in sensum Greg. Nyssenus in Orat. de Baptis. Christi: Panis, ait, initio communis est, sed per mysterium consecratus, vel sanctificatus, dicitur corpus Christi. Utrumque verò de nuda externa sanctitate verba facere, prior, appellatione vulgaris panis, i. e. destinato separatoque, per verbum & preces ad sanctum usum, contradistinguendi; posterior verò adjectis mox Similitudinibus nonnullis, à Sanctitate olei ad sanctum usum, aquæ in baptismate, quin templi lapidumque, ex quibus templum exstruendum est, petitis, disertè satis explicat.
latin.373: Denique (3) Substantiam terrestrem, singulari virtute divinâ, i. e. Spiritus Sancti efficacia, imprægnatam quasi, in S. Coena sistunt Theodoretus seu potiùs Clemens in Epitome Stromat. quæ desiderantur, dicens: Panem & oleum sanctificari τῇ δυνάμει τῶν ὀνομάτων, non eadem manentia κατὰ τὸ φαινόμενον, sicut in speciem assumpta sunt, sed δυνάμει εἰς δύναμιν πνευματικὴν μεταβάλλεσθαι — virtute in virtutem spiritualem mutari. Hæc Clementis dicta fusiùs declarat Victor Antiochenus ad illa Marci: Et cænantibus ipsis: Deus sese accommodans nostris infirmitatibus immittit propositis speciebus virtutem vitæ & ea transmutat in efficaciam ipsius carnis, ut in participationem vivificam eam habeamus. Prorsus ad mentem Liturgiæ Græcorum quam S. Marci vocant, utpote in qua rogatur Deus, ut immittat super panes & calices Spiritum Sanctum suum, & eos sanctificet & perficiat tanquam Deus omnipotens & faciat panem quidem corpus calicem autem sanguinem. Cujus quoque vestigia legit S. Cyprianus, Spiritum Sanctum non Autorem duntaxat Rei Sacramento debitæ esse, sed & sacramento plenitudinem gratiæ suæ infundere dicit, de Baptismo Christi. At, omnes hi, effatis his suis, Corporis Christi in S. Coena praesentiam, non aliam, quam spiritualem, tum per Autorem Spiritum, tum per Autoris hujus operationem, effectumque spiritualem, introducunt.
latin.374: Itaque recitata hactenus dicta Patrum aliaque similia quàm plurima, quibus equidem Eucharistiam sacram duplici substantia constare illi dixerunt, sed de legitimo tantùm usu intellexerunt, in quo, dignè accedentes, non terrestrem solum panem, sed & Cælestim participant, panem Eucharisticum precibus quidem sanctificari, sed ea sanctificatione, quâ omnia alia, perhibente Apostolo 1. Tim. 4. virtutem quidem ac efficaciam divinam, pani, vel affundi, vel infundi, à Spiritu Sancto, sed respectu duntaxat eorum qui pane sacramentali ritè vescuntur (utpote qui soli, non autem panis, δυνάμει εἰς δύναμιν virtute in virtutem spiritualem, per spiritualem corporis Christi participationem, transmutantur); Hæc inquam dicta Patrum, Rhetoricô præterea elata stylô, nec ad Metaphysicum rigorem exigenda, illuc, per errorem, traxerunt Consubstantiationem enixuri & interpretati sunt, acsi Patres Corporalem Unionem panis & corporis Christi, in Coena Sacra, etiam ante, & extra usum, seu perceptionem panis fidelem, fieri inculcassent, ex opere operato, vescenti cuivis, virtutem spiritualem, quin ipsam corporis Christi substantiam, corporali modo, conciliaturam ac communicaturam.

pass_a.369: §. III. The History of either Consubstantiation, to be handed down through some little Compendium, we shall comprehend in three moments only, of which the first narrates Consubstantiation’s CONCEPTION; the Second, its NATIVITY; the Third, its DURATION.
pass_a.370: We judge the CONCEPTION is to be located in a triple error of those who have at length pressed either Consubstantiation. Of these errors the FIRST is discharged by badly understood Sayings of the earliest Fathers, hinting that the sacred Eucharist consists either of two things, that is Substances, earthly and celestial, or of one earthly substance only, yet increased by some Celestial Accident — either of External Holiness or of Intrinsic Divine Virtue.
pass_a.371: (1) Two Substances here Irenaeus (A.D. 160), one for all, remembers: The bread, he says, which is from the earth, receiving the invocation of God, is now no longer common bread, but Eucharist consisting of two things, earthly and celestial (Against Heresies bk. 4 ch. 34); but in bk. 5 ch. 12, repeating nearly the same, he adds nonetheless that he wants his words restricted to the use of the sacred Eucharist, in which it comes about that just as celestial souls are nourished by celestial substance as by their proper food, so terrestrial bodies are nourished and grow by terrestrial substance: That Cup, he says, which is a creature, He confirmed as His blood, and that bread which is a creature as His body: When therefore cup and bread receive the word of God, the Eucharist of the blood and body of Christ comes about, from which the substance of our Flesh is increased and consists.
pass_a.372: (2) An earthly substance affected with a certain holiness is at least implicitly introduced by a Writer a little older than Irenaeus, St. Justin Martyr, when near the end of the Second Apology to Emperor Antoninus he recounts his time’s Christian custom of celebrating the Supper thus: After the President has given thanks and the people have acclaimed, those who among us are called Deacons or Ministers give to each of those present what they may take of bread and wine; and this food is called by us Eucharist; for we do not take them as common bread, nor as a common cup. To the same sense Gregory of Nyssa in the Oration on the Baptism of Christ: Bread, he says, is at first common, but consecrated or sanctified through the mystery is called the body of Christ. That both speak of bare external holiness — the former by the name common bread, i.e. to be contradistinguished as destined and set apart by word and prayers for holy use; the latter by similitudes soon added from the holiness of oil for holy use, of water in baptism, even of the temple and stones from which a temple is to be built — he explains plainly enough.
pass_a.373: Finally (3) Theodoret, or rather Clement in the Epitome of the Stromata that are wanting, sets in the Sacred Supper an earthly substance as if impregnated with a singular divine virtue, i.e. the efficacy of the Holy Spirit, saying: Bread and oil are sanctified by the power of the names, not remaining the same according to appearance as they were taken into species, but by power are changed into spiritual power. Victor of Antioch declares these sayings of Clement more fully on Mark’s And as they were eating: God accommodating Himself to our infirmities sends into the proposed species the virtue of life and transmutes them into the efficacy of His own flesh, that we may have it unto vivifying participation. Exactly to the mind of the Greeks’ Liturgy called of St. Mark, in which God is asked to send His Holy Spirit upon the breads and cups, and sanctify and perfect them as almighty God and make the bread indeed body and the cup blood. St. Cyprian also reads its traces, saying the Holy Spirit is not only Author of the Thing owed to the Sacrament but also pours into the sacrament the fullness of His grace (On the Baptism of Christ). But all these, by these their utterances, introduce no other presence of Christ’s Body in the Sacred Supper than a spiritual one — both through the Author Spirit and through this Author’s operation and spiritual effect.
pass_a.374: Therefore the Fathers’ sayings recited thus far and very many like them — by which indeed they said the sacred Eucharist consists of a double substance, but understood only of legitimate use, in which those who approach worthily participate not only terrestrial bread but also Celestial; that Eucharistic bread is indeed sanctified by prayers, but with that sanctification by which all other things are, the Apostle witnessing in 1 Tim. 4; that divine virtue and efficacy is poured or infused into the bread by the Holy Spirit, yet only with respect to those who rightly feed on the sacramental bread (inasmuch as they alone, not the bread, are transmuted by power into spiritual power through spiritual participation of Christ’s body) — these sayings of the Fathers, moreover elevated in a Rhetorical style and not to be pressed to Metaphysical rigor, those about to press Consubstantiation have by error drawn thither and interpreted as if the Fathers had inculcated a Corporal Union of bread and Christ’s body in the Sacred Supper even before and outside use, or faithful perception of the bread, about to reconcile and communicate by the work worked, to whoever eats, spiritual virtue — nay the very substance of Christ’s body — in a corporal mode.

369: §.III: both kinds of Consubstantiation get a short history in three moments.
370: CONCEPTION sits in a triple error of those who finally pressed either Consubstantiation.

FIRST error: early Fathers badly read — as if the Eucharist were two substances (earthly + celestial), or one earthly substance plus some celestial accident of external holiness or intrinsic divine virtue.
371: (1) Irenaeus (A.D. 160) is the stock witness for two things, earthly and celestial, in the Eucharist after invocation.

But bk. 5 restricts the saying to use: celestial souls feed on celestial substance; earthly bodies on earthly — the creature-cup and creature-bread confirmed as His blood and body when they receive God’s word.
372: (2) Justin (near Irenaeus’s senior) describes deacons giving bread and wine called Eucharist — not taken as common bread or cup.

Gregory of Nyssa: bread starts common, then consecrated is called Christ’s body — both mean bare external holiness (set apart by word and prayer; like oil, baptismal water, temple stones), not a second metaphysical substance.
373: (3) Clement (via Theodoret’s Stromata epitome): bread and oil change by the power of the names into spiritual power — not same in appearance.

Victor of Antioch, the Liturgy of St. Mark, and Cyprian speak of the Spirit sending life-virtue into the species — yet all introduce only a spiritual presence of Christ’s body, by the Spirit’s authorship and effect.
374: Those Father-sayings meant legitimate use: the worthy receive earthly and celestial; 1 Tim. 4 sanctification; Spirit’s virtue toward communicants, not a changed bread-substance.
Rhetorical, not metaphysical — yet consubstantiation-pressers twist them as if the Fathers taught corporal bread–body union before and outside faithful use, ex opere operato to any eater.
Stop before §.IV (SECOND error — middle-ages Fathers after Chalcedon).
